newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan financial reforms make analysts wary.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan financial reforms make analysts wary.

text.p: Pakistani analysts reacted warily on Tuesday to a reform plan for the state-run financial sector unveiled by the caretaker government.
They said the plan, spelled out to reporters on Monday by economic adviser Shahid Javed Burki, would have to be implemented properly if it was to succeed.
It is aimed at a greater degree of efficiency, slashing mounting bad debts of state-run banks and financial institutions and helping the process of privatisation.
"These are all proposed plans. We just have to wait and see how much of it is going to be implemented," Naunman Sheikh, senior analyst at KASB & Co, told Reuters.

According to a document obtained by Reuters, the government has decided to abolish the state-owned Pakistan Banking Council and merge the state-owned Regional Development Finance Corporation with the National Development Finance Corporation and an equity participation fund with the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan.

The document did not give any time frame for the mergers but said the Youth Investment Programmes would be merged with the Small Business Finance Corporation. "It is proposed thereafter to accelerate the privatisation of these entities," it said.
Newspapers quoted Burki as saying all bad debts of the state-run banks and institutions would be acquired by a temporary body called the Resolution Trust Corporation which would pursue payment.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan's annual report for fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) reported total debts of state-owned banks and financial institutions at 113.2 billion rupees in June 1996, compared with 101 billion rupees in the year-earlier period.
Burki said the recovery drive would be helped by stricter foreclosure laws and special banking tribunals and courts.
"The government would prepare comprehensive laws on foreclosure, another on banking tribunals and special banking courts...to facilitate recoveries of bad loans," the document said.
Sheikh said the foreclosure law would allow banks to confiscate property and other assets of defaulters before going to court for settlement or rescheduling of the loan.
"This will certainly help in discouraging wilful defaulters, who in the past have been defaulting on their dues and it was for the banks to approach courts for settlement," Sheikh said.
But Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said implementation of such strict laws would be difficult.
"Most of the defaulters are those who carry political clout. It will remain to be seen if any action is taken against such people," Aziz said.
He said unless the plans were followed up by privatisation of the institutions, the bad debts problem would return.
Burki said some bad debts may be marketed as long-term government securities or 10-year maturity bonds so that some of the burden could be shared.
Aziz said the plan for transfer and legal status of such bonds was not clear, but such schemes had been helpful in handling debt problems in Latin America.
